source.title: Kernel Regression with Infinite-Width Neural Networks on Millions of Examples
source.authors: Ben Adlam; Jaehoon Lee; Shreyas Padhy; Zachary Nado; Jasper Snoek

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied text contains the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law measurements to neural-kernel regression on image datasets, measuring held-out error as dataset size changes; it does not study language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work as background, but reports its own scaling results for image neural kernels. Those results bear on V5 and, for variation by architecture/evaluation data and the low-data slope transition, V7. It does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream task predictability.
record.test_reason: The paper measures held-out MSE of neural-kernel regression as image training-set size grows over about 6 orders of magnitude, and fits dataset-scaling exponents. This is a new setting, image models with infinite-width kernels, so it bears on V5. The exponents vary with setup and the curves bend at small sizes, which bears on V7. Parameter and compute scaling are not studied.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that neural kernels scale remarkably well, that their scaling curves suggest more data would help, and that the exponent grows with kernel complexity and with how in-distribution the eval data is. They also report a state-of-the-art kernel result on CIFAR-10 (91.2% with 20× augmentation) and competitive protein and molecule results.
record.recipe_differences: Measures dataset-size scaling of image neural-kernel regression errors, rather than language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents vary with kernel architecture and evaluation-set distribution. Small dataset sizes have a different slope; the augmentation curves for FC3 and Tuned Myrtle also change slope around factor 1.0. Tiny ImageNet exponents differ between 32×32 and 64×64 inputs.
record.problems: The evidence concerns neural-kernel image regression rather than language models or pretraining loss. Scaling exponents are presented in figures without uncertainty estimates. The results are specific to the tested datasets and kernel architectures.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating small-run fits to much larger runs. The authors' remark that more data could help is not tested.
Shape at fixed parameter count. Kernels are nonparametric.
Parameter or compute scaling, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. A quantified power law for augmented data is also absent, as are scaling curves for the protein and molecule tasks.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Fitting method, parameter counting, training schedule, compute-optimal split, and disagreement among published LM laws.

missing.what: CV8 data-augmentation curve, for which the text reports no noticeable slope change at factor 1.0, unlike FC3 and Tuned Myrtle

record.verdict_notes: The setting is infinite-width kernel regression, not trained networks. Only dataset-size scaling is studied, and no exponent uncertainties are given. The V7 links rest on exponents varying with architecture and data choices; these rows do not test fitting-method choices.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting much larger language-model runs from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its scaling with compute.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count in language models.
Tests image neural-kernel regression, including dataset-size scaling and image augmentation; does not test video, language models, repeated epochs as such, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.

Does not test language-model fitting choices, parameter counting, training schedules, compute-optimal allocation, or whether published language-model laws disagree; its setup-dependence evidence concerns image neural kernels.

rows.subject: Myrtle
rows.operation_detail: Varied Tiny ImageNet training dataset size and measured scaling at two image resolutions.
rows.note: The paper reports consistent power-law scaling from a sufficiently large dataset size.
rows.check: The subject is Tuned Myrtle (Figure 3 title), not Myrtle. The 32×32 vs 64×64 resolution changes the exponent (0.04 vs 0.06).

rows.subject: Myrtle
rows.operation_detail: Varied Tiny ImageNet training dataset size and measured scaling at two image resolutions.
rows.note: The paper reports consistent power-law scaling from a sufficiently large dataset size; full-resolution accuracy is reported as 44.7%.
rows.check: The subject is Tuned Myrtle (Figure 3 title), not Myrtle. The record's note on 44.7% accuracy is a test-set accuracy, not a scaling value.

rows.subject: FC3, CV8, and Myrtle (all cases)
rows.operation_detail: Compared scaling slopes across CIFAR-5m training-set sizes.

conditions.value: extremely small sizes, 10–100 examples, versus larger sizes

rows.measure: Slope of held-out loss/error scaling curve
rows.value: The small-size cases commonly have a lower slope, then transition to a more consistent, higher slope.
rows.note: This is the paper's aggregate description across the plotted cases; the stated transition qualifies a single power-law description across the entire range.
rows.check: State is fine. The paper says power-law behaviour holds across 4-5 orders of magnitude after the small-data (10-100 examples) transition.

rows.subject: FC3
rows.operation_detail: Varied CIFAR-10 training-set augmentation factor and measured classification error.

conditions.value: horizontal flip and RandAug; factor sweep

rows.measure: Classification-error curve slope versus augmentation factor
rows.note: The text states there is a noticeable change in slope around augmentation factor 1.0 for FC3; the figure shows both evaluation sets.
rows.check: This measures classification error against augmentation factor, with no power-law fit or exponent. The slope change near 1.0 coincides with the switch from i.i.d. subsets to augmented data, so it is not a single-curve bend relevant to V7. The removed V7 link was unjustified.

rows.subject: Tuned Myrtle
rows.operation_detail: Varied CIFAR-10 training-set augmentation factor and measured classification error.

conditions.value: horizontal flip and RandAug; factor sweep

rows.measure: Classification-error curve slope versus augmentation factor
rows.note: The text states there is a noticeable change in slope around augmentation factor 1.0 for Tuned Myrtle; the figure shows both evaluation sets.
rows.check: Same as r13: no exponent or fit. The slope change near factor 1.0 marks the change from real subsets to augmented data, not curve bending on one data type.

relationships.condition: Neural-kernel regression on CIFAR-5m (FC3, CV8, Myrtle) and Tiny ImageNet (Tuned Myrtle), beyond very small dataset sizes
relationships.reason: Held-out MSE follows power laws in dataset size, with αD 0.04-0.13 over 4-5 orders of magnitude (r1-r11).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out MSE followed data-size power laws with exponents of 0.04–0.13 over 4–5 orders of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Extremely small CIFAR-5m training sets (10-100 examples)
relationships.reason: All cases show a lower slope before moving to a consistent power law, so one power law does not cover the full range (r12).
relationships.display_finding: All tested cases had shallower slopes at 10–100 examples before entering a consistent power-law regime, preventing one power law from covering the full range.

relationships.condition: Across kernel architectures, evaluation sets and input resolution
relationships.reason: The exponent rises with kernel complexity (FC3 < CV8 < Myrtle on the same eval), with closer-to-training eval data, and with 64×64 vs 32×32 resolution (r1-r11).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents increase from FC3 to CV8 to Myrtle, with evaluation data closer to training data, and at 64×64 rather than 32×32 resolution.

relationships.reason: The curves bend from a lower to a higher slope around 10-100 examples, departing from a single power law (r12).
relationships.display_finding: CIFAR-5m curves transition from lower to higher slopes around 10–100 examples, departing from a single power law.
